column2: Both. javac compiles source code ahead of time into bytecode, which is the same on every platform. At runtime, the JVM interprets that bytecode, and it JIT-compiles hot methods into native machine code using profiling data (counts of what actually runs).
The JVM runs bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus the standard libraries. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, jcmd and jstack.
Bytecode is the same on every platform. Only the JVM implementation is different for each platform.

Code starts in the interpreter. Hot methods are compiled quickly by C1, which also collects profiling data. The hottest methods are compiled again by C2 with aggressive optimisations. If an assumption becomes invalid, the code can be deoptimised back to the interpreter.

column1: Why does Integer a = 128, b = 128; a == b print false?
column2: Integer.valueOf caches only −128 to 127. So 128 creates two separate objects, and == compares references, not values.

column1: What is autoboxing and what does it cost?
column2: The compiler adds valueOf() and xxxValue() calls to convert between primitives and wrappers for you. The costs are: a new object for values outside the cache, extra memory, more GC pressure, and a possible NullPointerException when unboxing null.

column1: When would you use Integer instead of int in an entity or DTO?
column2: When the value can genuinely be missing, like a nullable column or an optional field. An int would quietly default to 0, and 0 may be a valid business value, so you could not tell "missing" from "zero".
Generics work only with reference types because of type erasure (1.16). After compilation, the element type becomes Object, and an Object can't hold a primitive.

column1: What happens on integer overflow in Java?
column2: The value wraps around silently, using two's complement — no error is thrown. When overflow is possible, use long, Math.addExact/multiplyExact (which throw instead), or BigInteger.

column1: Why should you never use double for money?
column2: Binary floating point can't store most decimal fractions exactly, so every calculation adds a small rounding error, and these add up. Use long in minor units (paise) or BigDecimal with an explicit rounding mode.
When both are large, lo + hi can overflow and give a negative number. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 can't overflow.

Four reasons. It makes the string pool possible, because shared copies can't be changed. It allows a cached hash code, which makes Strings fast map keys. It gives thread safety without synchronisation. And it helps security, because a value can't be changed after it has been validated.

column1: Where is the String pool and how do strings get into it?
column2: It is a table in the heap (since Java 7). Literals and compile-time constants are added when the class loads. Strings created at runtime are added only if you call intern().

column1: How many objects does new String("abc") create?
column2: Up to two. One is the pooled literal "abc", if it isn't pooled already. The other is the new heap object.

column1: What changed in Java 9 for Strings?
column2: Compact strings: a byte[] plus a coder flag stores Latin-1 text in 1 byte per character. Also, concatenation now compiles to invokedynamic (StringConcatFactory), which performs better.

String is immutable. StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronised — it is fast and the default choice for building strings. StringBuffer is mutable and synchronised — it is a legacy class and slower.
Not inside one expression, because the compiler optimises it. The problem is repeated += across loop iterations, which is O(n²).
When its internal array is full, it grows to about double the old capacity plus 2 and copies once. This gives amortised O(1) appends — fast on average.
Always pass-by-value. For objects, the value that gets copied is the reference. So the called method can change the object, but it can't make the caller's variable point to a different object.

column1: What lives on the stack and what on the heap?
column2: The stack holds per-thread frames with local variables, primitive values and references. The heap holds all objects and arrays; it is shared across threads and managed by the GC.
Each thread has its own stack, so local variables are never shared between threads. But the objects they point to can still be shared.

column1: What is the order of initialisation in Java?
column2: First the static parts — parent then child, once, when the class is initialised. Then, for each new object: the parent's instance initialisers and constructor, then the child's instance initialisers and constructor.

column1: Can a constructor be private, and why would it be?
column2: Yes. It is used for singletons, utility classes, static factory methods like List.of, and builders that force you to create the object through build().

column1: What does final mean on a field, method, class?
column2: On a field: it is assigned only once, and it also gets safe-publication guarantees (other threads see it correctly set). On a method: it can't be overridden. On a class: it can't be extended.

column1: Why shouldn't constructors call overridable methods?
column2: The subclass's override runs before the subclass's fields are initialised. So it sees default values (null or 0) instead of the real ones.

column1: What is encapsulation and why does it matter?
column2: It means hiding state behind methods that enforce the invariants (rules that must always hold). So the object is always valid, and you can change the internals without breaking callers.
Package-private is visible only inside the same package. protected is visible in the package too, and also to subclasses in other packages.
Not by themselves. A setter for every field exposes state just like a public field does. Real encapsulation exposes meaningful operations that keep the invariants true.

Overloading means the same method name with different parameters; the compiler picks one at compile time using the declared types of the arguments. Overriding means a subclass redefines a method with the same signature; the JVM picks one at runtime using the actual object type, through dynamic dispatch.

column1: Can you override static or private methods?
column2: No. Static methods are hidden, not overridden — the compiler picks them by the reference type. Private methods are not inherited at all, so a method with the same name in a subclass is simply a new, separate method.

column1: How does the JVM decide which overridden method to call?
column2: It looks at the object's runtime class and finds the method in that class's virtual method table (via the invokevirtual instruction). If the JIT sees only one implementation at that call site, it may inline the call for speed.
An overriding method is allowed to return a subtype of the parent method's return type. For example, Dog clone() can override Animal clone().

column1: Interface vs abstract class, and how do you choose?
column2: Use an interface for a contract that many classes — possibly unrelated — implement, and when you need multiple inheritance of type. Use an abstract class when related classes share state and implementation, especially with a template method.
To let interfaces grow — for example, adding stream() to Collection — without breaking every existing implementation.

column1: Can an interface have a constructor or instance fields?
column2: No. It can have only constants, plus abstract, default, static and private methods.

column1: What happens if a class inherits the same default method from two interfaces?
column2: The code does not compile unless the class overrides that method. Inside the override, it can call one of them with InterfaceName.super.method().
Less coupling to the parent's implementation details. Flexibility at runtime, because you can swap collaborators. No fragile base class problems. And you control exactly which API you expose.

column1: Give an example where inheritance broke something.
column2: A HashSet subclass that counts additions double-counts, because addAll calls add internally and both are overridden. Composition avoids depending on the parent's internal self-calls.

column1: When is inheritance the right choice?
column2: When there is a true, stable is-a relationship with shared behaviour, or when a framework class is explicitly designed to be extended.
Equal objects must have equal hash codes. Equal hash codes do not require the objects to be equal. equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive and consistent, and must return false for null.

column1: What happens if you override equals but not hashCode?
column2: Two equal objects usually get different hash codes and land in different buckets. So HashMap.get and HashSet.contains fail, and sets accept logical duplicates.

column1: What happens if two unequal objects have the same hashCode?
column2: That is a collision. They share a bucket, and equals tells them apart. Everything stays correct, but lookups slow down if collisions happen often.

column1: Why should map keys be immutable?
column2: If a field used in hashCode changes after insertion, the entry stays in its old bucket. Lookups now compute a different bucket, so the entry can't be found — and it leaks.
Comparable defines a class's single natural ordering, written inside the class. Comparator defines external orderings; you can combine them, and the class itself does not need to change.

column1: Why not write return a - b?
column2: Because it can overflow for large values or values with mixed signs. Then the result has the wrong sign and the sort order is wrong.

column1: What does "consistent with equals" mean and why does it matter?
column2: It means compareTo returns 0 exactly when equals returns true. Sorted collections use compare to decide uniqueness, so if the two disagree, distinct elements get dropped or merged.

column1: Which algorithm does List.sort use, and is it stable?
column2: TimSort — a stable mix of merge sort and insertion sort, with O(n log n) worst case.

column1: How do you make a class immutable?
column2: Make the class final and all fields private final. Provide no setters. Make defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs. And return new instances for any change.
Their state never changes after safe construction. So threads reading at the same time can never see half-updated state, and no locks are needed.

column1: Is a class with only final fields immutable?
column2: Not necessarily. A final reference can still point to a mutable object — a list, an array, a Date — and that object must be protected too.

Checked exceptions extend Exception (but not RuntimeException), and you must declare or handle them. Unchecked exceptions extend RuntimeException and represent programming errors or conditions you can't recover from.

Yes, after try/catch — even when there is a return. The exceptions are System.exit, a JVM crash or an infinite loop. Also, a return inside finally overrides any exception or return value from the try block.
In try-with-resources, if close() throws after the body already threw, the close exception does not replace the main one. Instead it is attached to the main exception using addSuppressed.

column1: Should you catch Exception or Throwable?
column2: Catch the most specific type you can actually handle. Use a catch-all only at top-level boundaries, for logging and translating errors. Never swallow Errors like OutOfMemoryError (OOM).
The compiler checks generic types, then replaces type parameters with their bounds and inserts casts. So generic type information is not available at runtime.

column1: What can't you do because of erasure?
column2: You can't use primitives as type arguments, create a T or a T[], use instanceof with a parameterised type, or overload methods that differ only in their type arguments.
Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Use ? extends T when the structure produces values that you read. Use ? super T when it consumes values that you write.

column1: Why isn't List<String> a subtype of List<Object>?
column2: Because generics are invariant. Otherwise you could insert non-String objects through the List<Object> reference and corrupt the list.
A static nested class has no reference to an outer instance, so you can create it on its own. An inner class silently holds a reference to its outer instance and needs one to be created.

column1: How can an inner class cause a memory leak?
column2: Its hidden reference to the outer object keeps the outer object — and everything it references — reachable for as long as the inner object lives.

column1: Why must captured local variables be effectively final?
column2: Lambdas and inner classes capture a *copy* of the value. If later changes were allowed, the copy and the original would drift apart, which is confusing — and across threads it would cause race conditions.
The JVM guarantees exactly one instance per constant and thread-safe initialisation. It also blocks reflection and serialisation from creating extra copies.

column1: Can enums have constructors, fields and methods?
column2: Yes. Constructors are automatically private, and each constant can override methods with its own behaviour.

column1: Why store enums as strings in the database?
column2: Ordinals change when constants are reordered or inserted, and that silently corrupts stored data. Names are stable and readable.
It defines how long an annotation lives: SOURCE (only for the compiler), CLASS (in the bytecode, but not at runtime), or RUNTIME (available through reflection, which frameworks need).
It scans classes, reads their annotations, finds constructors and fields, creates and injects beans, and builds proxies. It caches this metadata for performance.

column1: What are the downsides of reflection?
column2: Slower calls, broken encapsulation, loss of compile-time safety, and problems with the module system and native images.

column1: Which collection would you use for X?
column2: Decide by how the data will be accessed: random access by index → ArrayList; lookup by key → HashMap; sorted order or ranges → TreeMap; take the min or max again and again → PriorityQueue; first-in-first-out (FIFO) or last-in-first-out (LIFO) → ArrayDeque.

column1: Why is Map not part of the Collection interface?
column2: A map holds key-value pairs and works through keys. It does not fit the Collection contract, which is about single elements added with add(E). Instead, a map gives you collection *views* of itself: keySet, values and entrySet.
When the array is full, it creates a new array 1.5× larger and copies the elements over. Because it grows by a multiple each time (geometric growth), adding at the end is amortised O(1).
10. It is created lazily, only on the first add.

column1: Time complexity of get, add, add(index), remove(index)?
column2: O(1), amortised O(1), O(n), O(n).

ArrayList is a contiguous array: O(1) random access, amortised O(1) append, cache-friendly, and low memory. LinkedList is a chain of nodes: O(1) insert/remove at the ends or at a position you already hold, but O(n) access by index and high memory use. Choose ArrayList by default.
When you insert or remove often at an iterator position inside a large list, or when you need a Deque that allows nulls. In other cases, ArrayDeque or ArrayList wins.

It is an array of buckets whose length is always a power of two. The key's hashCode is spread (h ^ h>>>16) and masked to get an index. Keys that collide form a linked list in the bucket; that list becomes a red-black tree when a chain reaches 8 and the table has 64+ buckets. A lookup compares the hash first, then equals. When size goes above capacity × 0.75, the table doubles, and each node either stays at i or moves to i + oldCap, decided by one bit.

column1: Why is HashMap O(1) and when isn't it?
column2: A good hash spreads keys evenly, so each bucket holds about one entry; a lookup is just index arithmetic plus one or two comparisons. It gets slow when many keys collide because of a poor hashCode — O(n) per bucket, or O(log n) once the bucket becomes a tree.

column1: Why must the capacity be a power of two?
column2: So that (n-1) & hash can replace the slower modulo (%), and so that a resize can split each bucket by checking a single bit.

Long chains are turned into trees (treeification); new nodes are added at the tail instead of the head, which fixed Java 7's infinite loop during concurrent resize; and the hash spreading was simplified.

column1: Can HashMap have a null key?
column2: Yes, one. Its hash is treated as 0, so it is stored in bucket 0. Values can be null too. ConcurrentHashMap allows neither null keys nor null values.

column1: What happens when two keys have the same hashCode?
column2: Both go into the same bucket, and equals tells them apart. Both are stored and found correctly — it just costs one extra comparison.
A doubly linked list runs through all the entries. It keeps insertion order by default, or access order when accessOrder is true.

column1: How do you build an LRU cache in Java quickly?
column2: Extend LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true, and override removeEldestEntry to return size() > capacity.
No — even reads change the order. Synchronise access to it, or use Caffeine or ConcurrentLinkedHashMap-style libraries.

TreeMap keeps keys sorted, is O(log n), has navigation methods (floor, ceiling, ranges), needs Comparable keys or a Comparator, and allows no null keys. HashMap has no order, is O(1) on average, and uses hashCode/equals.
A red-black tree — a self-balancing binary search tree (BST) with height ≤ 2·log₂(n+1). So every operation is O(log n) even in the worst case.

column1: How would you find the latest price effective at a given time?
column2: Store the price changes in a TreeMap keyed by effective time, and call floorEntry(time).
It wraps a HashMap. Elements are stored as keys with one constant dummy value. Uniqueness comes from how the map treats keys — the same key cannot be stored twice.
HashSet: no order, O(1). TreeSet: sorted, O(log n). LinkedHashSet: insertion order, O(1).

column1: Why prefer ArrayDeque over Stack and LinkedList?
column2: Stack is old, synchronised code that extends Vector. LinkedList creates a node object for every element. ArrayDeque is a cache-friendly circular array with O(1) amortised operations at both ends.
Inside, null is used to mark empty slots. Also, poll/peek return null to say "the deque is empty".
As an array-based binary min-heap. offer and poll are O(log n) using sift-up and sift-down, and peek is O(1).

column1: Why use a min-heap of size k to find the k largest elements?
column2: The root is the smallest of the current top k. Each new element either replaces the root in O(log k) or is thrown away. So the total time is O(n log k), and memory is only O(k).
No. Only the head is guaranteed to be the minimum.

column1: What is ConcurrentModificationException and when is it thrown?
column2: A fail-fast iterator throws it when the collection was structurally changed after the iterator was created, by anything other than the iterator itself. It detects this using modCount.

Fail-fast iterators throw CME when the collection is changed during the loop (ArrayList, HashMap). Fail-safe or weakly consistent iterators work on a snapshot, or put up with changes, without throwing (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap).

column1: How do you remove elements while iterating?
column2: Use Iterator.remove() or Collection.removeIf, or collect the items to remove first and remove them after the loop.
The first is a read-only view: the original list can still change, and the changes show through the view. The second is an independent immutable copy.

column1: What sorting algorithms does Java use?
column2: Dual-pivot quicksort for arrays of primitives, and TimSort (which is stable) for objects and lists.

column1: What is the gotcha with Arrays.asList?
column2: The list has a fixed size and is backed by the array, so add/remove don't work. And if you pass a primitive array, you get a list with one element: the array itself.
It is an interface with exactly one abstract method. You can use it as the target of a lambda or a method reference. The @FunctionalInterface annotation makes the compiler check this rule.

column1: How are lambdas implemented — are they anonymous classes?
column2: No. The compiler moves the body into a private synthetic method. The lambda object is created through invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory the first time that line runs. Non-capturing lambdas are cached and reused as singletons.

column1: Why must captured variables be effectively final?
column2: The lambda captures a copy of the value, not the variable. If you could change the variable later, the copy would be out of date. It would also invite data races when the lambda runs on another thread.

column1: Function vs Supplier vs Consumer vs Predicate?
column2: Function takes T and returns R (T→R). Supplier takes nothing and returns T (()→T). Consumer takes T and returns nothing (T→void). Predicate takes T and returns a boolean (T→boolean).

column1: What is lazy evaluation in streams?
column2: Intermediate operations only build the pipeline; nothing runs until a terminal operation is called. Then each element flows through all the stages, one element at a time. This allows short-circuiting and avoids temporary collections between stages.
Intermediate operations return a stream and are lazy. Terminal operations produce a result or a side effect, and they start the execution.
map is one-to-one: one element in, one element out. flatMap maps each element to a stream and then flattens all those streams into one stream.
No. After a terminal operation the stream is consumed, and using it again throws IllegalStateException. Create a new stream from the source instead.
There are two cases. Duplicate keys without a merge function throw IllegalStateException. Null values throw an NPE.

column1: How do you count elements per category?
column2: Use groupingBy(classifier, counting()).
partitioningBy always splits into exactly two groups, true and false, using a predicate. groupingBy creates as many groups as there are distinct keys.

A Spliterator splits the source into chunks. Each chunk runs as a ForkJoin task on the common pool, and idle threads use work stealing to pick up extra tasks. Finally the partial results are combined.

column1: When are parallel streams a bad idea?
column2: With small data; with I/O or other blocking work; with shared mutable state; with order-dependent operations; with sources that split poorly; and inside servers, where the common pool is shared by everything.
To make "value may be absent" visible in the API signature. It forces callers to handle the empty case, so you get fewer NullPointerExceptions.
orElse evaluates its argument eagerly, even when a value is present. orElseGet calls the supplier only when the Optional is empty.
In fields, method parameters and collections, and in performance-critical inner loops.

column1: Why is java.time better than Date/Calendar?
column2: It is immutable and thread-safe. It keeps exact instants separate from local and zoned values. Its API is clear, and its formatter is thread-safe.
Instant is one exact moment on the UTC timeline. LocalDateTime is a wall-clock value with no zone, so it can mean different moments in different places.

column1: How do you make time-dependent code testable?
column2: Inject a Clock and call now(clock). In tests, pass Clock.fixed(...) so time does not move.
Private final fields, a canonical constructor, accessor methods, and equals/hashCode/toString that use all components.

Records are part of the language, they are immutable, and they need no annotation processing. @Data generates mutable getters and setters, and it needs the Lombok library. Use records for DTOs and value objects.

column1: Can a JPA entity be a record?
column2: No. JPA needs a no-arg constructor, mutable fields, and classes it can subclass to create proxies.
To restrict which classes can extend a type. This makes the hierarchy closed and known to the compiler, so pattern-matching switches can be checked for exhaustiveness.

column1: What does pattern matching for switch add?
column2: It allows type patterns, record deconstruction and guards (when) in case labels. The compiler also checks exhaustiveness over sealed types.

column1: How does this compare to the Visitor pattern?
column2: It reaches the same goal — one operation per variant — without the boilerplate of double dispatch (the accept/visit back-and-forth calls). A new operation is just a new method with a switch.
No. The type is inferred once, at compile time, and then it is fixed. var only removes the repeated type name from the declaration.
It returns a value from a block-style arm ({ ... }) of a switch expression.

column1: What are the headline features of Java 21?
column2: Virtual threads; record patterns and pattern matching for switch (now final); sequenced collections; and generational ZGC. There are also previews of structured concurrency and scoped values.

A process has its own memory space. Threads live inside a process: they share its heap, but each has its own stack and program counter. So threads are cheaper to create and to switch between. The cost is that shared data needs synchronisation.
start() creates a new thread, and that new thread executes run(). If you call run() directly, it simply executes on the current thread, like a normal method call.

NEW (created, not started). RUNNABLE (running or ready to run). BLOCKED (waiting to get a monitor lock). WAITING / TIMED_WAITING (waiting for a signal, or for a signal or a timeout). TERMINATED (finished).

column1: How do you stop a thread correctly?
column2: Cooperatively. You interrupt it (or set a volatile flag), and the task checks the flag and exits by itself. When the task catches InterruptedException, it must either restore the flag or exit.

It is a correctness bug where the result depends on the timing, or interleaving, of threads that use shared mutable state. A classic example is lost updates when many threads run count++ at the same time.

Atomicity means other threads see an operation either fully done or not done at all — never half-done. Visibility means a write by one thread can actually be seen by other threads. Locks give both. volatile gives visibility only.
It is a read-modify-write made of three steps. Two threads can interleave those steps, so updates get lost.

column1: Explain how ThreadPoolExecutor handles a new task.
column2: If fewer than core-size threads are running, it starts a new core thread. Otherwise it puts the task in the queue. If the queue is full, it starts a non-core thread, up to the max size. If it is already at max, it rejects the task through the rejection handler.
It uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Under overload, tasks keep piling up until you hit OutOfMemoryError. They are never rejected and the callers are never slowed down.

column1: How do you size a thread pool?
column2: For CPU-bound work, about the number of cores. For I/O-bound work, about cores × (1 + wait/compute). Then check it with Little's Law and load tests. Finally, keep it within what downstream systems can handle, such as the DB pool size.

column1: What is CallerRunsPolicy and why is it useful?
column2: When the pool is full, the thread that submitted the task runs it itself. That keeps the producer busy, so it slows down. You get simple back-pressure without dropping any work.
Callable returns a value and can throw checked exceptions. Runnable returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions.
get() blocks. There are no callbacks. You can't chain or combine Futures. You can't complete one manually. CompletableFuture solves all of these.
Two things. Mutual exclusion on the monitor: only one thread at a time. And visibility: everything written before releasing the lock is seen by the next thread that acquires it.
sleep is a static Thread method. It pauses the thread but does not release any locks. wait must be called while holding the monitor. It releases the monitor and waits for a notify or a timeout.

column1: Why must wait() be called in a loop?
column2: Spurious wakeups are allowed — a thread can wake without a notify. Also, the condition may have changed between the notify and the moment the thread gets the lock back. So it must check again.

column1: Is synchronized reentrant? Why does it matter?
column2: Yes. A thread can re-enter locks it already holds. So synchronized methods on the same object can call each other without deadlocking on themselves.
Visibility: writes are seen by all threads. And ordering: no reordering across the volatile access. It does not make compound operations atomic.

It is the JMM's ordering guarantee: if A happens-before B, then B sees A's effects. It is created by locks, volatile, thread start/join, executor hand-offs and concurrent collections. It is also transitive.

column1: Why does double-checked locking need volatile?
column2: Without it, the reference can be published before the constructor finishes. Another thread may then use a partly constructed object.
volatile gives visibility only. synchronized gives mutual exclusion plus visibility for a whole block. AtomicInteger gives lock-free atomic operations on a single variable, with visibility.

ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeouts, interruptible acquisition, optional fairness and multiple Conditions. But you must unlock it yourself in finally. synchronized is simpler and is released automatically.
AbstractQueuedSynchronizer. It is the framework behind most j.u.c locks and synchronisers. It uses an int state changed by CAS, and a FIFO queue of parked threads.

column1: When would you use a ReadWriteLock?
column2: For shared data that is read a lot and written rarely. Reads can then run at the same time, and only writes are exclusive.
A fair lock serves threads in arrival order: no starvation, but slower. A non-fair lock lets new threads jump in (barging) for higher throughput. Non-fair is the default.
An atomic CPU instruction. It sets a memory location to a new value only if it currently holds the expected value. It is the base of lock-free algorithms and Java atomics.
With a retry loop. It reads the volatile value, tries a CAS to value+1, and retries if the CAS fails.
LongAdder splits (stripes) the count across several cells to reduce contention. So increments are much faster with many threads. The cost is that sum() is slower and is not an atomic snapshot.
CAS can't detect that a value changed and then changed back. You solve it with versioned references, like AtomicStampedReference.

column1: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety in Java 8?
column2: Reads are lock-free because the fields are volatile. Inserting into an empty bin uses CAS. Writing to a non-empty bin uses synchronized on that bin's first node only. Resizing is cooperative — threads that hit a forwarding node help move bins. And the size is kept in striped counters, so counting is not a bottleneck.

column1: Why doesn't it allow null keys or values?
column2: In a concurrent map, if get returned null, you could not tell "key absent" from "key mapped to null". You also cannot check both with containsKey and get atomically, because another thread may change the map in between. So null is banned and always means "absent".

column1: HashMap vs Hashtable vs synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap?
column2: HashMap has no synchronisation, so it is unsafe for concurrent writes. Hashtable and synchronizedMap use one lock for every operation, so all access goes one at a time. ConcurrentHashMap allows reads in parallel with no lock, and writes in parallel with fine-grained, per-bucket locking.

column1: Is map.get(k) + map.put(k, v+1) safe on ConcurrentHashMap?
column2: No. Each call on its own is atomic, but the pair is not — another thread can update between them and you lose its update. Use merge(k, 1, Integer::sum) or compute to do it in one atomic step.

A latch lets one or more threads wait for N events, and it is one-shot — it cannot be reset. A barrier makes N threads wait for each other. It is reusable for the next round, and it can run an action once all threads arrive.

column1: What is a Semaphore used for?
column2: It limits how many threads can use a resource at the same time. For example, at most N parallel calls to a partner API, or at most N DB-heavy jobs running together.
A lock has one owner and gives mutual exclusion — only one thread inside at a time. A semaphore has N permits and no owner, so any thread may release a permit.
Future only gives you a blocking get and cancel. CompletableFuture adds non-blocking callbacks, chaining, combining results, timeouts, completing it yourself from code, and proper exception handling.
thenApply transforms the value, like map. thenCompose chains a function that returns another CF and flattens the result, like flatMap. thenCombine merges the results of two independent CFs.

The thread that completes the previous stage runs it. If the stage is already complete, your calling thread runs it immediately. thenApplyAsync instead runs it on the executor you pass (or the common pool if you pass none).

column1: How do you handle errors in a CF chain?
column2: Use exceptionally to recover with a value, handle to map both success and failure, and whenComplete for side effects like logging. Remember that exceptions arrive wrapped in CompletionException.

column1: What are virtual threads and how do they differ from platform threads?
column2: They are lightweight threads managed by the JVM. Their stacks live on the heap, and many of them share a few carrier OS threads. When blocked on I/O they unmount and free the carrier, so millions can exist. Platform threads, in contrast, map one-to-one to expensive OS threads.
Pinning is when a virtual thread cannot unmount from its carrier. In Java 21 this happens inside synchronized or native code. If it blocks there, it holds the carrier thread for the whole wait.

column1: Do virtual threads make code faster?
column2: They increase throughput — total requests handled — for I/O-bound concurrency, because OS threads are not tied up during waits. They do not make a single request faster, and they do not speed up CPU-bound work.
No. They are cheap to create, so use one per task. Limit access to scarce resources with semaphores instead.

column1: What are the four conditions for deadlock?
column2: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. All four must be true at the same time for a deadlock to happen.
Break one of the conditions. The usual ways: take locks in one consistent global order, use tryLock with timeouts and backoff, take all resources at once, or use lock-free designs.

column1: How do you detect a deadlock in a running JVM?
column2: Take a thread dump with jcmd Thread.print or jstack. The JVM reports Java-level deadlocks and names the threads and locks involved. To check from code, use JMX: ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads().

Deadlock: threads are blocked forever, each waiting on the other. Livelock: threads are active and busy, but make no progress. Starvation: one thread is always denied the resource while the others keep making progress.

Use a circular array, one ReentrantLock and two Conditions (notFull and notEmpty). Wrap each await in a while loop to re-check after waking up. After each put, signal notEmpty; after each take, signal notFull (see the code above).

column1: Why use two Conditions instead of wait/notifyAll?
column2: Producers wait on notFull and consumers wait on notEmpty. So each signal wakes only the right kind of thread, and no time is wasted waking threads that can't proceed.

column1: How do you shut down consumers cleanly?
column2: Send poison-pill messages, one per consumer. Or interrupt the threads, and have them exit when they catch InterruptedException.

ArrayBlockingQueue is always bounded, uses one lock, and allocates its array up front, so memory use is predictable. LinkedBlockingQueue is optionally bounded and uses separate put and take locks for higher throughput, but it allocates a new node for every element.

Each Thread holds a ThreadLocalMap. Its keys are weak references to the ThreadLocal objects, and its values are strong references to the data. get simply looks up the value in the current thread's map.

column1: Why can ThreadLocal cause memory leaks or data leaks?
column2: Pooled threads live forever. So a value that is set and never removed stays there across tasks. This leaks memory, and can even leak one request's data into the next request.

column1: How does Spring's @Transactional know which connection to use?
column2: TransactionSynchronizationManager binds the connection or EntityManager to the current thread using a ThreadLocal. The repositories then look it up there. That is also why a transaction does not follow your work onto other threads.

column1: How do you pass context to async tasks?
column2: ThreadLocals don't move to other threads automatically. So capture the value before you submit the task, then set it at the start of the task and clear it at the end. A TaskDecorator or a context-propagation library can do this for you.

When a class loader is asked for a class, it first passes the request to its parent. It loads the class itself only if the parent cannot find it. Because of this, core classes always come from the bootstrap loader, so nobody can spoof them and there are no duplicate copies.

CNFE: a class that was requested dynamically by name (for example Class.forName) is not found. NCDFE: a class that was available at compile time cannot be loaded at runtime — either it is missing, or its static initialisation failed earlier.

On its first active use: creating an instance, calling a static method, reading a static field that is not a compile-time constant, using reflection, or initialising a subclass. Reading a compile-time constant does not trigger it, because the value is copied into the caller at compile time.

column1: What are the JVM memory areas?
column2: The heap (young generation with Eden and two survivor spaces, plus the old generation), Metaspace, the code cache, per-thread stacks and PC registers, native method stacks, and direct memory.
Metaspace, in Java 8. It lives in native memory and grows automatically, so the old fixed-size PermGen out-of-memory errors went away. Interned strings moved to the heap.

column1: Why does a Java process use more memory than -Xmx?
column2: -Xmx limits only the heap. Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache, direct buffers and GC data structures all come on top of it.

column1: Why is the heap divided into generations?
column2: Because most objects die young. Collecting a small young generation often is cheap, since only the few survivors are copied. Long-lived objects sit in the old generation, which is collected rarely.

column1: How does an object move to old gen?
column2: By surviving a number of minor GCs — it ages each time it is copied between survivor spaces. It can also go there directly if it is too large, or if the survivor spaces overflow.
A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer: a private chunk of Eden for one thread. The thread allocates objects by just moving a pointer forward, with no synchronisation.

column1: How does the JVM decide an object is garbage?
column2: If it cannot be reached from any GC root — thread stacks, static fields, JNI references, active threads — it is garbage. Unreachable cycles are collected too.

column1: What is a stop-the-world pause and a safepoint?
column2: A stop-the-world pause is a phase where all application threads are halted so the GC can work safely. Threads stop at safepoints, which are points where the JVM knows the exact state of their stacks.

Mark-sweep frees dead objects in place, which leaves fragmentation. Mark-compact moves live objects together, so there are no gaps. Copying evacuates live objects to a fresh area; its cost is proportional to the amount of live data.

G1 is region-based. It evacuates mostly during stop-the-world pauses and aims for a pause target of tens of milliseconds, giving a good balance with throughput. ZGC compacts concurrently using load barriers. Its pauses stay under a millisecond regardless of heap size, but it costs some throughput and CPU.
After concurrent marking, it evacuates first the old regions that contain the most garbage. This gets back the most space for each pause.

column1: Which collector for a batch job vs a low-latency API?
column2: Parallel for batch throughput. G1 by default for services. ZGC when pause times threaten the latency SLO.
A weak reference is cleared at the next GC once the object is reachable only through weak references. A soft reference is cleared only when memory is under pressure.
It holds keys through weak references. When a key is no longer reachable from anywhere else, the GC clears it and the map removes that entry.

Yes. A leak is an object that stays reachable but is no longer needed. Common causes: unbounded caches, static collections, listeners and ThreadLocals that are never removed, lambdas or inner classes holding outer references, and unclosed resources.

column1: How do you recognise a leak from metrics?
column2: Heap usage right after GC rises steadily over time. GC frequency and duration grow. Eventually you get an OOM. A restart resets it, but only for a while.

column1: CPU is at 100% on a Java service. What do you do?
column2: Find the hot threads with top -H. Convert their TIDs to hex and match them to the nid in thread dumps taken a few seconds apart. Read their stacks. Check whether the busy threads are GC threads, which would point to a memory problem. Profile with JFR or async-profiler. Then fix the hot code path.

column1: Requests are hanging. How do you investigate?
column2: Take thread dumps to see what the threads are waiting on — locks, connection pools, sockets without timeouts, or deadlocks. Then correlate that with traces and pool metrics.

column1: How do you investigate an OutOfMemoryError?
column2: First identify the OOM type. Check the GC logs for the heap-after-GC trend. Compare class histograms taken some time apart. Analyse the heap dump's dominator tree and the paths to GC roots. Fix the reference that is holding the memory. Then verify with metrics.
The memory that would be freed if an object were collected. It includes the object itself and everything that is reachable only through it.

Java Flight Recorder. It is a built-in event recorder with low overhead. It captures CPU samples, allocations, GC, locks and I/O, and you analyse the recording in JDK Mission Control. It is safe to run in production.

It profiles running code and compiles hot methods into optimised native code, first with C1 and then C2. It uses inlining, devirtualisation, escape analysis and loop optimisations. If its assumptions break, it deoptimises.

column1: Why do Java services need warm-up?
column2: Code starts in the interpreter. The JIT needs profiling data and time to compile the hot paths. Caches and connection pools also need time to fill up.
A JIT analysis that proves an object does not escape its method or thread. This allows the JIT to skip the allocation entirely (scalar replacement) and to remove locks on it (lock elision).

column1: How does the JVM behave in containers?
column2: It is container-aware. It reads the cgroup CPU and memory limits and uses them to size the heap, the GC threads and thread pools. You should set MaxRAMPercentage to about 70–75%, to leave room for non-heap memory.

column1: A pod keeps restarting with exit code 137 but no Java OOM in the logs. Why?
column2: The kernel OOM-killed it. The total process memory — heap plus metaspace, threads and direct buffers — went over the container limit. Fix it by lowering the heap percentage or raising the limit, and check native memory usage with NMT (Native Memory Tracking).

Spring is the IoC container plus its family of modules. Boot is an opinionated layer on top of it — it makes default choices for you. It adds starters, auto-configuration, externalised config, an embedded server, executable JARs and Actuator, so an app needs almost no setup.
It combines three annotations: @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan. The component scan starts from the annotated class's package and goes downward into its sub-packages.

It is a dependency bundle that brings everything needed for one capability (web, JPA, security), with versions that work together. Having it on the classpath also triggers the matching auto-configuration.

IoC means the container, not your code, controls creating objects and connecting them. DI means dependencies are given to the object through the constructor, a setter or a field, instead of the object creating them itself. This gives loose coupling, easy testing and one central place for configuration.
Dependencies are explicit and immutable, objects are never partly initialised, unit tests are easy without Spring, and circular dependencies fail early at startup.

column1: How does Spring resolve which bean to inject?
column2: First by type. If several beans match, it uses @Primary, then @Qualifier, then the parameter name matching a bean name. If none of these decides it, startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.

column1: How do you fix a circular dependency?
column2: Refactor the design: move the shared responsibility into a new bean, or reverse one dependency using an interface or events. Only as a last resort, use @Lazy injection.

@Component marks your own class so component scanning picks it up. @Bean is a factory method inside a @Configuration class; you use it for third-party types or when building the object needs custom logic.

All three register beans. @Service is only a label that shows meaning. @Repository also adds persistence exception translation — it converts database exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException types.
So that when one @Bean method calls another, it gets back the container's singleton instead of creating a new instance.

column1: Two beans implement the same interface. How does Spring choose?
column2: First @Primary, then @Qualifier, then the parameter name. If none of these decides it, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. If you want all of them, inject List<T> or Map<String, T>.

column1: How do you implement the Strategy pattern with Spring?
column2: Make each strategy a bean that implements a common interface. Then inject Map<String, Strategy> or a List, and build a registry keyed by type to pick the right strategy at runtime.
singleton (the default), prototype, request, session and application — plus websocket.
Only if you make them so. Spring does not synchronise them. Keep them stateless, or use thread-safe fields.

column1: What happens when a prototype is injected into a singleton?
column2: It is injected only once, so the singleton always uses the same instance. To get a fresh one, use ObjectProvider, @Lookup, or a scoped proxy.
Spring's singleton is one instance per container, so several contexts mean several instances. The GoF Singleton is one per class loader, and the class itself enforces it.

Instantiate → inject dependencies → Aware callbacks → BPP before-init → @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet / init-method → BPP after-init (this is where proxies are created) → in use → @PreDestroy / destroy on shutdown.
A BFPP changes bean definitions (the recipes) before any bean is created. A BPP changes or wraps each bean instance, around the time it is initialised.
In postProcessAfterInitialization, by the auto-proxy creator BeanPostProcessor. The proxy then replaces the raw bean in the container.
Spring creates proxies — CGLIB subclasses or JDK interface proxies — inside a BeanPostProcessor. The proxy runs the advice around each call and then passes the call to the target bean.

column1: Why doesn't @Transactional work when I call the method from the same class?
column2: The internal call goes through this, not through the proxy, so the transaction interceptor never runs. Move the method to another bean, or use TransactionTemplate.
A JDK proxy can only implement interfaces. CGLIB creates a subclass of the class, and it is Boot's default. Because it subclasses, final classes and final methods can't be advised.
@Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After (runs always, like finally), and @Around (wraps the call and decides whether and when to proceed).

column1: How does Spring Boot resolve a property that's defined in several places?
column2: By property-source precedence. Command-line arguments beat environment variables. Environment variables beat profile-specific files. Profile-specific files beat application.yml.
@Value injects one value at a time by its string key. @ConfigurationProperties loads a whole prefix into a typed object that can be validated. It is better for groups of related settings.
Never in source control. Inject them through environment variables from Kubernetes Secrets, or from a vault (Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault), and rotate them regularly.

column1: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?
column2: Starters put auto-configuration classes on the classpath, listed in AutoConfiguration.imports. Each class applies only if its @Conditional checks pass. It backs off if you have already defined that bean yourself.

column1: How do you see why something was or wasn't auto-configured?
column2: Run with --debug to get the condition evaluation report, or use Actuator's /conditions endpoint.

column1: How do you disable a specific auto-configuration?
column2: Use @SpringBootApplication(exclude = …) or spring.autoconfigure.exclude in properties. Or simply define your own bean of that type.

column1: What happens when a Spring Boot application starts?
column2: Spring prepares the environment, creates the context, and loads bean definitions (scan, config, auto-config). Then it creates the singletons, running post-processors and creating proxies. It starts the embedded server, runs the runners, and finally fires ApplicationReadyEvent.
Yes, by default — they run on the publisher's thread. Add @Async to handle them asynchronously. @TransactionalEventListener ties delivery to a transaction phase, such as after commit.
So users are never told about changes that later roll back. For guaranteed delivery across services, use an outbox instead.

column1: What happens when a request hits a Spring Boot app?
column2: Tomcat gives the request a thread from its pool. Then servlet filters run, such as security. Next the DispatcherServlet takes over: HandlerMapping finds the controller method, interceptors run, and the HandlerAdapter prepares the method arguments — Jackson turns the JSON into objects and validation runs. Then the controller runs, and a message converter writes the response as JSON. If an exception is thrown anywhere, @ControllerAdvice handles it.
It is Spring MVC's front controller — one single servlet that receives every request. It sends each request to the right handler using mappings, adapters, resolvers and converters.

PUT replaces the whole resource and is idempotent — repeating it gives the same result. PATCH updates only some fields. POST creates something or triggers an action, and it is not idempotent unless you add an idempotency key.

column1: Which status code for a business-rule failure such as insufficient points?
column2: 422 Unprocessable Entity — the input is fine but the rule says no. Use 409 if it is a conflict with the current state. 400 is for input that is malformed or invalid.

column1: Why not return JPA entities from controllers?
column2: Because of lazy-loading exceptions, accidental N+1 queries, infinite recursion on two-way mappings, leaking internal fields, and tying the API to the database schema.

column1: How does @Valid work in Spring MVC?
column2: After Jackson turns the body into an object, Spring calls Bean Validation on it. Any broken rule throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which you map to a 400 response.

column1: How do you write a custom validator?
column2: Create a constraint annotation marked with @Constraint(validatedBy = …), and write a class that implements ConstraintValidator<A, T>.isValid.
In the service or domain layer, because that layer has the data and context to decide. Annotations are only for checking the shape of the input.

column1: How do you handle exceptions globally in Spring?
column2: With a @RestControllerAdvice class that has @ExceptionHandler methods. Each one maps an exception type to a status code and a ProblemDetail body. Unexpected errors are logged once, there.

column1: Why doesn't my @ControllerAdvice catch an exception thrown in a filter?
column2: Filters run before the DispatcherServlet, so Spring's exception resolvers are not involved yet. Handle it in the filter itself or in the security entry point.

A filter works at the servlet level. It runs for every request and can wrap the request and response. An interceptor works at the Spring MVC level. It runs around the chosen handler and can see its method and annotations.

column1: Where would you put tenant resolution and why?
column2: In a filter, early in the chain. Then every later component — security rules, controllers, repositories — has the tenant context. Clear it in finally so the next request on that thread starts clean.

column1: What timeouts do you configure on an HTTP client?
column2: Connect timeout, read/response timeout, and pool-acquisition timeout. All of them must fit inside the caller's latency budget.

RestTemplate is the old synchronous client. RestClient is the modern synchronous client with a fluent style. WebClient is reactive and non-blocking, used with WebFlux or for high-concurrency async calls.
To reuse pooled TCP/TLS connections, avoid handshake costs and port exhaustion, and keep timeouts and limits in one central place.

column1: JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA?
column2: JPA is the ORM specification — the rules and annotations. Hibernate is the implementation that actually does the work. Spring Data JPA sits on top of JPA and generates repository implementations from your interfaces.

column1: How does Spring Data create a repository implementation from an interface?
column2: At startup, it creates a proxy for the interface, backed by SimpleJpaRepository for CRUD. It parses method names, or reads @Query annotations, and turns them into queries.

IDENTITY uses the database's auto-increment. Hibernate must insert each row immediately to learn its ID, so batching is disabled. SEQUENCE fetches IDs in advance in blocks, so Hibernate can batch the inserts.

column1: What are the default fetch types?
column2: ToOne links (@ManyToOne, @OneToOne) are EAGER. ToMany links are LAZY. You should set ToOne links to LAZY explicitly.

column1: What is the owning side of a relationship?
column2: It is the side that holds the foreign key (@JoinColumn). JPA writes the relationship to the database from this side. mappedBy marks the other side, the inverse side.
When the link has its own data or its own lifecycle. Then model the join table as an entity, with two ManyToOne relations.
It is Hibernate's first-level cache and unit of work, one per transaction. It maps IDs to managed entity objects, keeps a snapshot of each, and flushes changes at commit.
At flush, Hibernate compares each managed entity with its snapshot. For every changed entity, it generates an UPDATE automatically.

column1: Do you need to call save() after modifying an entity?
column2: Not for a managed entity inside a transaction — the change is flushed at commit. save matters only for new or detached entities.
persist makes a new object managed. merge copies a detached object's values onto a managed object (loading it first if needed) and returns that managed object.
One query loads N parent rows. Then reading a lazy link on each parent fires one more query per parent. That is N+1 queries in total.
Use fetch joins, @EntityGraph, batch fetching (default_batch_fetch_size), or DTO projections that select exactly what is needed. Detect it by logging and counting the SQL.

column1: Why is join fetch with pagination dangerous?
column2: When you fetch a collection, Hibernate cannot apply LIMIT in SQL. So it loads all the rows and does the paging in memory.
Touching a lazy link that is not loaded yet, after its persistence context (session) has closed. This usually happens outside the transaction.

column1: What is Open-Session-in-View and why disable it?
column2: It keeps the persistence context open for the whole web request, so lazy loading works in the view layer. But it hides queries outside transactions and holds a DB connection for the full request. Disable it and load data explicitly in services.

A proxy's TransactionInterceptor begins a transaction through the PlatformTransactionManager and binds the connection to the current thread. Then it calls the method. At the end, it commits, or rolls back according to the rollback rules.

column1: What are the default rollback rules?
column2: Roll back on RuntimeException and Error. Commit on checked exceptions, unless rollbackFor says otherwise.

column1: List cases where @Transactional is silently ignored.
column2: Self-invocation, private or final methods, objects not managed by Spring, work on other threads, and the wrong transaction manager. Also, it still commits when a checked exception is thrown or an exception is swallowed.

column1: Why shouldn't you call external APIs inside a transaction?
column2: The DB connection and locks stay held while you wait on the network. This hurts throughput and risks pool exhaustion and deadlocks. Also, if the DB transaction fails, you cannot roll back the external effect.

REQUIRED joins the current transaction, or creates one; everything shares it. REQUIRES_NEW pauses the current one and runs a separate transaction that commits or rolls back on its own. NESTED creates a savepoint inside the current transaction.
For work that must be saved no matter what happens to the caller, such as audit or failure logs. But remember it needs an extra connection.

column1: Why might REQUIRES_NEW cause a deadlock?
column2: Each request holds one connection and needs a second. If such requests fill the whole pool, they all wait for each other forever.

column1: Name the isolation levels and the anomalies each prevents.
column2: Read uncommitted prevents none. Read committed prevents dirty reads. Repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads. Serializable also prevents phantoms and write skew.

column1: What is a lost update and how do you prevent it?
column2: Two read-modify-write transactions overwrite each other's result. Prevent it with an atomic UPDATE statement, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or an optimistic version check.

column1: What is the default isolation in PostgreSQL and MySQL?
column2: PostgreSQL uses READ COMMITTED. MySQL InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ.

Optimistic finds clashes at write time with a version check. It takes no locks and retries on conflict, so it suits low contention. Pessimistic locks rows at read time (FOR UPDATE) and blocks other writers, so it suits high contention.

column1: How would you prevent double-spending of points under concurrency?
column2: Use an atomic conditional UPDATE (balance >= amount) and check the affected row count — or use a row lock. Add an idempotency key so duplicate requests are not processed twice.

column1: What happens when an optimistic lock check fails?
column2: The update affects zero rows, and Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException. The application then retries, or returns 409.

column1: How do you size a connection pool?
column2: Start small, about 10–20 per instance. Keep the total under what the DB can handle. Then tune from pool metrics and DB load. The DB's cores and I/O limit useful parallel work — not the number of app threads.

column1: Why not use ddl-auto=update in production?
column2: It is not versioned, and it cannot do safe data migrations. It may make destructive or locking changes, and it can behave differently in each environment. Use Flyway/Liquibase migrations, and set validate.

column1: How do you make a schema change with zero downtime?
column2: Use expand-migrate-contract. Make additive changes first, write to both old and new, backfill in batches, switch reads to the new structure, and remove the old structure in a later release.

column1: How does Spring Security process a request?
column2: A FilterChainProxy runs the matching SecurityFilterChain. First, authentication filters check the credentials, build an Authentication object and store it in the SecurityContextHolder. Then authorisation filters check the URL rules. Security exceptions are turned into 401 or 403 responses. Finally, method security checks like @PreAuthorize run at the service proxy.
Authentication checks who you are; if it fails, you get 401. Authorisation decides what an already-authenticated user may do; if it fails, you get 403.

column1: How do you enforce tenant isolation?
column2: Take the tenant from the verified token, not only from a header the client sends. Check it in method security. And apply a mandatory tenant filter to every data query, so even a missed check cannot return another tenant's rows.

The client sends a signed token with the request. The service checks the signature using the issuer's public key from the JWKS endpoint. It then checks expiry, issuer and audience, and builds the security context from the claims. There is no session lookup.

column1: How do you revoke a JWT?
column2: You cannot revoke it directly. So you keep access tokens short-lived and revoke the refresh tokens instead. For sensitive actions, use token introspection (ask the provider if the token is still valid) or keep a deny-list of token IDs (jti).
OAuth2 is delegated authorisation — it gives access tokens for calling APIs. OIDC is an identity layer on top of it — it adds ID tokens and user info, so you know who the user is.

column1: Which flow for a mobile app, and which for service-to-service?
column2: Authorization Code with PKCE for a mobile app. Client Credentials for service-to-service.
A stub just returns canned answers. A mock also lets you verify which calls were made. A spy wraps a real object and calls the real methods unless you stub them.
External boundaries and collaborators — repositories, HTTP clients, clocks and message publishers. Do not mock value objects or the logic you are testing.

column1: How do you test time-dependent code?
column2: Inject a Clock into the class. In tests, pass Clock.fixed so "now" is always the same.
@WebMvcTest is a web-layer slice with mocked services. @DataJpaTest is a JPA slice with repositories, each test in a rolled-back transaction. @SpringBootTest loads the full application context.

column1: Why use Testcontainers instead of H2?
column2: Your tests run against the same database engine and version as production. So they catch differences in SQL dialect, locking, constraints and features that H2 would hide.

column1: How would you test that concurrent redemptions never overdraw?
column2: Write an integration test against real Postgres. Fire N concurrent redemptions, each with a different idempotency key. Then assert the final balance and the exact number of successes.

column1: How does Spring Kafka deliver messages — exactly once?
column2: No — by default it is at-least-once. Offsets are committed after the listener returns, so a failure causes redelivery. So you make consumers idempotent. Kafka transactions give exactly-once only for Kafka-to-Kafka processing.

column1: How do you make a consumer idempotent?
column2: Store the processed event ID, with a unique constraint, in the same DB transaction as the business effect. Or make the effect itself idempotent, for example an upsert by business key.

column1: What is a dead-letter topic and when do you send to it?
column2: It is a separate topic for records that failed after all retries, or that can never succeed (validation or deserialisation errors). Moving them out stops them from blocking the partition. The DLT is monitored; records are fixed and replayed.

column1: How do you preserve ordering per account?
column2: Use the account ID as the record key. All of that account's events then go to one partition and are processed by one consumer thread, in order.
A proxy builds a key from the method arguments. On a hit, it returns the cached value without calling the method. On a miss, it calls the method and stores the result.

column1: Why evict on write instead of updating the cache?
column2: Updating can race with a concurrent read that reloads old data and writes it to the cache last, leaving stale data. Deleting forces the next read to load fresh data.
A local cache (Caffeine) is fastest, but each instance has its own copy and they can drift apart. Redis is shared and consistent across instances, but costs a network hop and serialisation.

Closed: calls flow normally and results are recorded. It moves to Open when the failure or slow-call rate crosses a threshold; now calls fail fast. After a wait, it moves to Half-open and allows a few trial calls. If they succeed, it goes back to Closed; if they fail, it goes back to Open.
Only idempotent operations that fail with transient errors — timeouts, 503s, connection resets. Use exponential backoff with jitter, a limited number of attempts, and ideally retry at one layer only.
It isolates resources per dependency, using a semaphore or a thread-pool limit. So one slow dependency cannot use up all your threads.

column1: How do these patterns prevent cascading failures?
column2: Timeouts limit how long you wait. Circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency. Bulkheads limit how many resources one dependency can use. Fallbacks keep the caller responsive.

column1: How does @Async work and what are its limits?
column2: A proxy hands the call to an executor and returns immediately. Limits: it does not work on self-invocation or private methods; it loses ThreadLocal context unless you propagate it; and the work is lost if the app crashes.

column1: How do you ensure a scheduled job runs once across multiple instances?
column2: Use a distributed lock (ShedLock on a DB or Redis), or leader election. Or run the job outside the app — a Kubernetes CronJob, or Quartz in clustered mode.

Metrics are aggregated numbers, used to detect problems and alert. Traces follow one request across services to find where the latency or error is. Logs are detailed events that explain what happened.

Liveness asks: is the process healthy, or should Kubernetes restart it? Readiness asks: can it serve traffic right now — is it warmed up and are its dependencies reachable? A failing readiness probe takes the pod out of load balancing without restarting it.
RED (rate, errors, duration) is for request-driven services. USE (utilisation, saturation, errors) is for resources such as pools, queues and CPU.

column1: Monolith vs microservices — how do you decide?
column2: Weigh the benefits — team size, clear domain boundaries, need for independent scaling and deployment — against the costs: operational complexity, network failure modes and data consistency. Start with a modular monolith, and split along bounded contexts when it is justified.

column1: How do services stay consistent without distributed transactions?
column2: Use local transactions plus events (the outbox pattern), sagas with compensation steps, idempotent consumers and reconciliation jobs. You accept eventual consistency.

column1: What does an API gateway do?
column2: Routing, authentication and token validation, rate limiting, TLS termination, request shaping, CORS, observability and canary routing. It should contain no business logic.

column1: How do OOP principles show up in your design?
column2: Encapsulation: each entity checks and protects its own rules (invariants). Abstraction: callers depend on interfaces such as PaymentGateway, not on concrete classes. Polymorphism: a new variant is just a new class. Inheritance: I use it only for a real is-a relationship; otherwise I use composition (one object holding another).

column1: What's an anaemic domain model and why is it a smell?
column2: It is a model where entities have only data plus getters and setters, and all the logic sits in services. It is a smell because no class owns the rules. So rules get copied into many services, or someone forgets them.

Both are has-a relationships. In composition, the whole owns the part's lifecycle — an order's lines are deleted with the order. In aggregation, the part lives independently — players still exist after a team is broken up.
Association is a lasting link in the structure, usually a field. Dependency is short-term use, usually a method parameter or a local variable.

Each class should have one reason to change. For invoices, I keep calculation (finance rules), persistence (database), PDF rendering and delivery (email) in separate classes. A workflow class coordinates them.

column1: Explain OCP with an example from your work.
column2: In our incentive and reward system, each new rule type is a new Strategy class, registered by its type name. The evaluation engine does not change when we add a type.

column1: What is LSP and give a violation?
column2: You must be able to use a subtype anywhere the base type is expected, without breaking correctness. Two classic violations: Square overriding Rectangle's setters so width and height change together, and a subclass that throws UnsupportedOperationException for a base-class method.
Clients should not depend on methods they don't use. So I prefer small, role-specific interfaces over one fat interface.
Both high-level and low-level modules depend on abstractions. The high-level (business) side owns these abstractions. The low-level details implement them and are injected from outside.

DIP is a design principle — it is about which direction dependencies point. DI (dependency injection) is a technique — you pass dependencies in from outside instead of creating them inside. Containers like Spring automate DI.

column1: How do you implement a thread-safe singleton?
column2: Use an enum singleton, or the holder idiom. Another option is double-checked locking with a volatile field.
They create global state that can change, hide dependencies, make testing hard and couple code tightly. A single instance supplied through dependency injection avoids these problems.
Factory Method lets subclasses decide one product type. Abstract Factory creates a whole family of related products through one interface.
A factory decides *which* class to create, usually in one step. A builder constructs *one* complex object step by step.

column1: When do you use a Builder?
column2: For complex objects with many optional parameters. It gives readable construction, validation inside build(), and an immutable result.

column1: Shallow vs deep copy in Prototype?
column2: A shallow copy shares the nested mutable objects with the original. A deep copy makes its own copies of them. I prefer immutable components or explicit copy constructors, so sharing is safe.
It converts one interface into a different interface that the client expects. It wraps the incompatible class and translates the calls, the data and the errors.

Decorators add behaviour at runtime by wrapping objects (composition), and you can combine them freely. Inheritance fixes behaviour at compile time, and you need a new subclass for every combination, so the number of classes explodes.
A Proxy keeps the same interface and controls access. A Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour. An Adapter changes the call to a different interface.

column1: What problem does a Facade solve?
column2: It hides a complex subsystem behind one simple interface. This reduces coupling, and clients no longer copy the same coordination code.
In rule trees that combine conditions with AND/OR, such as incentive schemes. Also in file systems and organisation charts.

They have the same structure. In Strategy, the client chooses the strategy, and it stays fixed for the whole operation. In State, the state objects themselves move the context to other states as events happen.
A new algorithm is just a new class, registered with the context. The context and the existing strategies do not change.

column1: Where is Observer used in Java/Spring?
column2: Spring application events and listeners, GUI listeners, and reactive streams. Across services, it becomes pub/sub messaging.

column1: When do you use the State pattern instead of an enum?
column2: When each state has its own distinct behaviour and transitions involve real logic. For a simple status machine, an enum with a transition table is enough.
Make each action a command with execute and undo. Keep an undo stack and a redo stack. When a new command is executed, clear the redo stack.

column1: Where is Chain of Responsibility used in Spring?
column2: Servlet filters and the Spring Security filter chain. HandlerInterceptors work in a similar way.
Template Method keeps a fixed skeleton and lets subclasses change individual steps (inheritance). Strategy swaps the whole algorithm by plugging in a different object (composition).

It turns business rules into predicate objects (yes/no checks) that you can combine with and, or and not. You can reuse them in memory or turn them into database queries, as Spring Data JPA Specifications do.

column1: How do you avoid over-engineering in an LLD round?
column2: Build the stated requirements simply (KISS/YAGNI). But put abstractions at the obvious places of variation that the interviewer mentioned. Then explain how you would extend the design.

column1: How do you approach an LLD problem?
column2: First, clarify the requirements and scope. Then identify the entities and their relationships. Define the interfaces, and choose patterns where things vary. Code the core flow end to end. Finally, handle edge cases, concurrency and extensions, and explain the trade-offs as you go.

column1: How do you check a win in O(1)?
column2: Keep one counter per row, per column and for both diagonals. Add +1 for X and −1 for O on the lines that pass through the played cell. If a counter reaches +N or −N, that player has won.

column1: How would you support K-in-a-row on an N×N board (K < N)?
column2: The full-line counters no longer work. Instead, after each move, start from the placed cell and count matching symbols in a row along the 4 directions (row, column, two diagonals). That costs O(K) per move — the work depends only on K.

column1: How would you add undo or a bot?
column2: For undo, use the Command pattern: push each move onto a stack, and to undo, pop it and reverse its counter changes. For a bot, add a MoveStrategy interface. Plug in different versions behind it — random, greedy, or minimax (a search that tries all future moves).

column1: How do you prevent two gates assigning the same spot?
column2: Take the spot with an atomic poll from a concurrent free-spot structure, one per spot type. A lock per spot type also works. If the spots live in a database, use SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (lock a free row and skip rows others have locked) or a conditional update like "set occupied where it is still free".

column1: How would you allocate the nearest spot to the entry gate?
column2: Keep, for each gate, a PriorityQueue/TreeSet of free spots sorted by distance from that gate. Hide it behind an AllocationStrategy interface so you can swap the rule later.

column1: How would you add weekend pricing or a monthly pass?
column2: Write new FeeStrategy implementations and pick one based on the date or the vehicle. The parking flow itself does not change.

column1: How does this change for 1,000 lots in a city?
column2: It becomes an HLD (high-level design) problem. Store the spot inventory in a database, per lot. Add a booking service that uses conditional updates so two bookings cannot take one spot. Cache availability so the "how many spots free?" reads are cheap.

column1: Why HashMap plus a doubly linked list?
column2: The map finds the node in O(1). The doubly linked list lets you remove a node from the middle and insert it at the front in O(1). It also gives O(1) access to the least recently used item at the tail. Neither structure can do all of this alone.

column1: How would you make it scale under heavy concurrency?
column2: Use lock striping: split the cache into N independent LRU segments, each with its own lock, and choose the segment by key hash. Threads on different segments don't block each other. The trade-off is that eviction is LRU per segment, so it only approximates a global LRU. Or use Caffeine, which buffers and samples accesses instead of locking on every read.

column1: How would you add a TTL?
column2: Store an expiry time in each node. On access, if the entry has expired, treat it as a miss and remove it. Clean up the rest either with a periodic sweep or lazily when you touch them.

LFU means *Least Frequently Used*. Keep two maps: key → (value, freq), and freq → LinkedHashSet of keys. The LinkedHashSet keeps insertion order, so among keys with the same frequency you evict the least recently used one. Also track the current minimum frequency, so eviction is O(1).

column1: How do you make logging not slow the application?
column2: Check the level first, so disabled logs cost nothing. Use parameterised messages, so the string is built only if the log is enabled. Use asynchronous appenders with a bounded queue, and a clear policy for what happens when it is full — drop or block.

column1: How would you support per-package levels like com.fa.loyalty=DEBUG?
column2: Use hierarchical logger names, split by dots. A logger takes the level of its nearest configured ancestor. So com.fa.loyalty.redeem gets DEBUG from com.fa.loyalty.

column1: How would you add request IDs to every line?
column2: Use an MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context). It is a ThreadLocal map — a map private to each thread. A request filter puts the request ID into it at the start, every LogEvent copies it, and the filter clears it after the request ends.

A token bucket allows controlled bursts while keeping a smooth average rate, and it needs only O(1) state per client. A sliding window log is exact, but it stores one timestamp per request. A sliding window counter gives a close estimate using just two counters.

column1: How would you make it distributed?
column2: Keep the state in Redis and update it with an atomic Lua script per key, so the read-and-update happens as one step (13.2). Another option: keep local buckets on each instance, and give each instance a share of the global quota.

column1: How do you clean up idle clients?
column2: Store the last-access time for each bucket. Remove buckets that have been idle longer than a TTL. Or simply use a cache with expireAfterAccess, which does this for you.

column1: How do you preserve ordering per key with multiple consumers?
column2: Give each worker its own queue. Send each job to a fixed worker using hash(key) % workers. All jobs for one key then go to one worker, which handles them in order. This is exactly how Kafka partitions keep per-key order.
Keep an attempt count in the job. On failure, put it back in the queue after a delay, using a DelayQueue or a scheduled executor. Retry up to N times. After that, move it to a dead-letter list.
So that overload causes back-pressure (producers wait) or rejection. Without a bound, the queue grows without limit and you get an OOM (OutOfMemoryError).
