Each state allows a different set of actions. If you put each state's behaviour in its own class, every transition is written clearly in one place, and illegal actions simply cannot happen — the state class rejects them.

column1: When does greedy change-making fail and what's the alternative?
column2: Greedy fails for *non-canonical* coin sets, where taking the biggest coin first is not always best. Example: coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6 — greedy gives 4+1+1 (three coins), but 3+3 (two coins) is better. The alternative is dynamic programming (DP) — the classic "coin change" problem — extended to respect the limited number of each coin in the cash box.

column1: How would you add UPI payment?
column2: Add a PaymentMethod strategy with implementations for coins, UPI and card. (A strategy is a swappable piece of behaviour behind one interface.) When any payment method completes, it moves the machine to the dispensing state.

column1: Which scheduling algorithm would you use and why?
column2: LOOK (or SCAN): serve all stops in the current direction, then reverse. It is efficient, and unlike "always go to the nearest request" it is *starvation-free* — no floor waits forever.

column1: How do you choose which elevator answers a hall call?
column2: Use a cost function that looks at distance, whether the lift is going the right direction, and its current load. Put it behind a DispatchStrategy interface, so you can swap in other strategies — for example, one tuned for peak hours or one that saves energy.

Use one controller thread that processes a queue of requests and ticks, one at a time. This is *actor style* — one owner of the data that handles messages in order. Because only one thread touches the shared state, there are no race conditions (bugs where two threads change the same data at once).

column1: How do you handle ₹100 split three ways?
column2: Work in paise: 3333, 3333 and 3334. Hand out the leftover paisa in a fixed, predictable way, so the shares always add up exactly to the total.

First work out each user's net balance. Then repeatedly pair the largest creditor with the largest debtor, using heaps — this runs in O(n log n). Mention that finding the exact minimum number of payments is NP-hard, so this greedy method is a good approximation, not a guaranteed best.

column1: How would you support groups and expense edits?
column2: Keep balances scoped to each group. Store expenses as immutable records, and treat an edit as a reversal of the old expense plus a new expense. Then either recompute the balances or apply just the differences (deltas).

column1: How do you prevent double booking?
column2: Check and hold all the requested seats *atomically* (all-or-nothing). In a single server, do this under a per-show lock. In a distributed system, use a conditional multi-row UPDATE and verify the updated row count, or use Redis SET NX.

Seats move to HELD, with a booking ID and an expiry time. If the user confirms within that window, the seats become BOOKED. When the hold expires — detected lazily on the next attempt, or by a sweeper job — the seats are released.

column1: What if payment succeeds after the hold expired and someone else took the seat?
column2: Mark the booking EXPIRED and trigger a refund. The payment callback handler must be idempotent, so a repeated callback does not refund twice or book twice.

column1: How do you prevent duplicate reward postings when events are retried?
column2: Store an idempotency key for each source event. Protect it with a unique constraint, saved in the same transaction as the ledger entry. If a duplicate arrives, return the existing entry instead of posting again.
Each accrual becomes a lot, with its remaining points and an expiry date. Redemptions use up the oldest lots first. Expiry then removes whatever is left in lots that are past their date.

column1: How do balance and ledger stay consistent?
column2: Both are updated in one transaction, so they change together or not at all. On top of that, a *reconciliation* job regularly checks, for each account, that the sum of the entries equals the cached balance.

column1: How would you let admins create rules without deployments?
column2: Store rule trees as data (JSON). When loading, parse them into Composite condition objects and payout strategies. Validate them when they are saved, and keep versions.

column1: How do you explain to a sales rep why they didn't qualify?
column2: Each node in the tree returns pass/fail plus a short description. The engine joins these into a full explanation and stores it with the outcome.

column1: How does this scale to hundreds of thousands of reps?
column2: Use pre-aggregated metrics per user and period. Run the evaluation in parallel — it is *stateless* (it keeps no data between calls), so it can be split by tenant across workers. Cache the scheme definitions so they are not loaded again for every rep (13.14).

column1: How do you make the game testable?
column2: I pass a Dice strategy into the game instead of creating dice inside it. In production it is random; in tests I pass dice that return a fixed sequence of rolls, so every test gives the same result.

column1: How would you add "roll again on a 6, three 6s forfeits the turn"?
column2: I would put this rule in the turn loop as a separate rule object, say TurnPolicy. The game asks the policy what happens after each roll. Then each rule variant is its own class, and you can plug in a different one without changing the game loop.

column1: How would you add partitions and ordering per key?
column2: Keep several logs per topic — each log is a partition. Choose the partition with hash(key) % partitions, so the same key always goes to the same partition. Ordering is then guaranteed within a partition, which means all messages for one key stay in order.

Subscribers in one group share the partitions between them. Each partition is read by only one member of the group. The group stores one shared offset per partition. Different groups are fully independent — each group gets every message.

If you move the offset after processing, you get at-least-once: nothing is lost, but a crash can cause duplicates. If you move it before processing, you get at-most-once: no duplicates, but a crash can lose a message. Because duplicates can happen, consumers should be idempotent — processing the same message twice must give the same result as processing it once.

All copies share the same details — title, author, ISBN — so those live once in Book. But each physical copy has its own status, location and loan history, so that lives in BookCopy. With one class you could not track several copies of the same title.

Each book has a FIFO (first-in, first-out) queue of members. When a copy is returned, it is held for the first member in the queue, and that member is notified. If they don't collect it before the hold expires, it passes to the next member in the queue.

column1: How would you search by title or author at scale?
column2: I would not scan every book. I would build an inverted index — a map from each word to the books that contain it — over the tokenised (split into words) titles and authors. In production, Elasticsearch does this for you.

column1: How do you guarantee a drink never partially consumes ingredients?
column2: I check all the ingredients and deduct all of them inside one critical section (one locked block). If any check fails, nothing is deducted. The alternative is one lock per ingredient, but then I must always take the locks in the same fixed order to avoid deadlock.

column1: How would you support N outlets?
column2: I use a fixed thread pool of N workers, or a semaphore with N permits. Orders are processed in parallel by these workers. The inventory is the one shared resource, and it is synchronised so only one thread changes the stock at a time.

column1: How would you add a new beverage or an add-on?
column2: A new beverage is just a new recipe entry — data, not code. An add-on is a decorator: it takes a base recipe and returns a new recipe with the extra ingredient quantities added.

column1: How do you prevent assigning one driver to two riders?
column2: Before offering the ride, I change the driver's status atomically. In memory, that is a CAS from AVAILABLE to ON_TRIP. In a distributed system, it is a conditional UPDATE in the database (update only if status is still AVAILABLE) or a Redis SET NX (set only if the key doesn't exist). Only one request can win.

column1: How do you find nearby drivers efficiently?
column2: I use a spatial index — a grid, geohash, H3 or quadtree — keyed by map cell. I search the rider's own cell first, then the rings of neighbouring cells, until I have enough candidates.
Every few minutes, I calculate the demand-to-supply ratio (riders requesting vs drivers free) for each area cell. Based on that ratio, I pick a multiplier and apply it through the PricingStrategy.

column1: How do you approach a system design question?
column2: First I clarify the functional and non-functional requirements and estimate the scale. Then I define the APIs and the data model and sketch the architecture. Next I go deep on the hardest components. Finally I discuss bottlenecks, failures and how the system grows — and I justify each choice with its trade-offs.

column1: How many QPS is 100 million requests per day?
column2: About 1,150 on average (10⁸ / 86,400). At a 3× peak, that is roughly 3,500.
Because the scale decides the architecture. It tells you whether one node is enough or you need sharding, how much caching you need, how much queue throughput you need, and what it will cost.

Vertical scaling adds resources to one machine. It is simple, but it has a limit and is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines. It has no hard limit and tolerates failures, but it needs stateless services and load balancing.
The instance keeps no client-specific state in its memory between requests. All state is moved out to databases, caches or tokens.
L4 routes connections by IP and port. It is fast and works with any protocol. L7 understands HTTP. It routes by path, header or cookie, and it terminates TLS.

column1: How does a load balancer know an instance is unhealthy?
column2: In two ways. Active health checks call the instance regularly — for example an HTTP readiness endpoint or a TCP check. Passive detection watches real traffic for errors or timeouts.

column1: What caching strategy would you use and why?
column2: Usually cache-aside with TTLs. It is simple, and the system still works if the cache fails. I delete the key on writes and add jitter to TTLs.

column1: How do you prevent a cache stampede?
column2: Use single-flight loading per key, locks, early refresh, serving stale data while one request refreshes it, and TTL jitter.

column1: Why delete instead of update the cache on writes?
column2: An update can race with a read happening at the same time. That read may put old data back into the cache after your update. If you delete instead, the next read loads fresh data from the DB.

column1: How does a CDN reduce latency?
column2: It serves cached content from edge locations close to users. So requests avoid the long round trip to the origin.

column1: How do you invalidate CDN content?
column2: Use versioned URLs (the preferred way), Cache-Control TTLs, or the CDN's explicit purge APIs.

column1: SQL vs NoSQL — how do you decide?
column2: I default to SQL, because it gives transactional integrity and flexible queries. I choose NoSQL only for a concrete need: massive write throughput, a flexible schema, simple key access at huge scale, or multi-region availability.

column1: Why might you use several databases in one system?
column2: Because each one serves a different access pattern — transactions, caching, search, analytics. I keep one source of truth and feed the others from it using events or CDC.

Synchronous replication waits for replicas to confirm each write. It is durable but makes writes slower. Asynchronous replication does not wait. It is fast, but replicas lag and recent writes can be lost on failover.

column1: What is replication lag and how do you handle it?
column2: It is the delay before replicas show the leader's writes. I handle it with read-your-writes routing (send a user's reads to the leader right after they write), lag-aware routing, or by accepting eventual consistency where that is fine.

In leaderless replication with N replicas, a write needs W acks and a read needs R responses, with R + W > N. Because the two sets must overlap, every read includes at least one replica with the latest successful write.

column1: How do you choose a shard key?
column2: It needs high cardinality and an even spread. It should match the main access path, so most queries hit one shard. For range sharding, avoid keys that always increase.
Cross-shard queries and joins, distributed transactions, rebalancing, hot shards, and more operational complexity.

Partitioning splits a table inside one database. It helps with pruning (skipping partitions a query doesn't need) and retention. Sharding spreads data across multiple database servers. It adds capacity and write scale.
During a network partition, you must choose consistency (reject or block some requests) or availability (serve data that might be stale). A payment ledger chooses C. A social feed chooses A.
It says that even with no partition, there is still a trade-off — between latency and consistency.

column1: Where would you use strong vs eventual consistency in a loyalty platform?
column2: Strong consistency for balances, redemptions and idempotency checks (checks that stop the same request being processed twice). Eventual consistency for leaderboards, analytics, notifications and search.

column1: What problem does consistent hashing solve?
column2: It keeps key movement small when nodes are added or removed. Only about 1/N of the keys move, instead of nearly all of them.
They spread each physical node's ranges all around the ring, which evens out the load. They also let you give bigger nodes more points, so they take a bigger share.

It decouples producers from consumers, so one being slow or down does not stop the other. It absorbs traffic spikes, retries failed work in the background, and fans out events to many consumers. Overall, the user path becomes more resilient and faster.

A queue hands out tasks and deletes each message once it is acknowledged; it has rich routing and per-message features like TTL, priority and DLQ. Kafka keeps an ordered log per partition that can be replayed. Many consumer groups read it independently, at very high throughput.

column1: What delivery guarantee do you design for?
column2: At-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, so duplicates are harmless. Exactly-once is possible only inside systems that support transactions end to end.
Only within a partition. So choose the message key so that events which must stay in order share the same key, and therefore the same partition.
The number of partitions. Each partition is read by at most one member of a consumer group, so extra members sit idle.

column1: How do you configure Kafka for no data loss?
column2: Replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, and producer acks=all with idempotence on. On the consumer side, commit offsets only after processing.
Kafka keeps only the latest record for each key, plus *tombstones* (a key with an empty value) to mark deletes. This turns the topic into a durable changelog of the current state.

column1: How do you make a POST endpoint idempotent?
column2: The client sends an idempotency key. The server stores the key and the response under a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the business effect. On a duplicate, it returns the stored response instead of doing the work again.

column1: How do you make a Kafka consumer idempotent?
column2: Save each processed event ID under a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the business effect. Or make the effect itself safe to repeat, such as an upsert or a conditional update.
Not across independent systems. Instead, you get exactly-once *effects*: deliver at least once, and make the processing idempotent.

column1: What is the dual-write problem and how does the outbox solve it?
column2: Writing to a database and to a broker can't be done as one atomic step, so one can succeed while the other fails. The outbox writes the event into a table in the same DB transaction as the change. Then a relay or CDC publishes it reliably, at-least-once.

2PC locks resources across all participants and gets stuck if the coordinator fails. Sagas use local transactions with compensating actions instead. You get eventual consistency without distributed locks, which is why sagas are preferred in microservices.

In choreography, services react to each other's events with no central coordinator; it is simple, but the flow is hidden. In orchestration, a coordinator drives the steps and compensations; it is explicit and easier to monitor and change.

column1: Where would you implement rate limiting?
column2: At the API gateway or edge for limits on clients, backed by a shared store like Redis so all instances see the same counts. Also inside your own clients, to respect outbound partner limits.

column1: What should an API gateway do and not do?
column2: It should do routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS, observability and request shaping. It should not contain business logic.

REST/JSON works everywhere, humans can read it, and it can be cached. gRPC is a typed, binary protocol on HTTP/2 with streaming and lower latency. So gRPC fits better for internal service-to-service calls.

column1: How do you paginate a large, changing dataset?
column2: Use keyset/cursor pagination on an indexed, unique ordering column. Return an opaque "next" cursor that the client sends back for the next page.

column1: How do you design reliable webhooks?
column2: Sign the payloads, retry with backoff, make receivers idempotent by keying on the event ID, and give a replay endpoint or dashboard.

column1: How would you handle large file uploads?
column2: Give the client a pre-signed URL so it uploads directly to object storage, using multipart/resumable upload for big files. Keep metadata in the DB, start processing from storage events, and deliver files through a CDN.

column1: Why not use the database for full-text search?
column2: A search engine has inverted indexes, analysers and relevance scoring. It handles fuzzy, multilingual, ranked search at scale far better than SQL. Feed it via CDC, and keep the DB as the source of truth.

column1: How do you prevent cascading failures?
column2: Use timeouts, limited retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding and graceful degradation. Together they stop one failing part from pulling down the services that call it.
RPO is the maximum data loss you can accept, measured in time. RTO is the maximum time you can take to restore service. Together they decide your replication, backup and failover design.

column1: Why do distributed locks need fencing tokens?
column2: A client can pause (because of GC or the network) and its lock can expire while another client takes the lock. A token that always increases lets the resource reject writes from the old, stale holder.
The SLI is the measured indicator. The SLO is the internal target for it. The SLA is the external promise in the customer contract.

column1: What is an error budget used for?
column2: It puts a number on how much unreliability is allowed. When it burns fast, alerts fire and feature releases slow down so the team can focus on reliability work.

column1: How do you ensure tenant isolation in a multi-tenant system?
column2: Take the tenant from the authenticated token, never from the request body. Enforce it in authorisation checks, and apply mandatory tenant filters at the data layer — or use separate schemas/databases for strong isolation. Add tests that try cross-tenant access.

column1: What security measures would you add to a payments or points system?
column2: Strong auth, idempotency, maker-checker for manual adjustments, audit logs, encryption, rate limits, anomaly alerts and reconciliation.

column1: How would you generate unique IDs across many servers?
column2: Use Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp + machine ID + sequence) or UUIDv7. Both are time-ordered and need no coordination. Use range leasing when IDs must be dense or short.

column1: Why are random UUIDs bad as primary keys in B-tree indexes?
column2: Random inserts land all over the index. This causes page splits, poor cache locality and larger indexes. Time-ordered IDs are added near the end of the index instead.

column1: Why NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN?
column2: If the subquery returns even one NULL, NOT IN returns no rows at all. NOT EXISTS gives the correct result in that case, and the database usually runs it as an efficient anti join.

column1: Nested loop vs hash vs merge join?
column2: Use a nested loop when the outer input is small and the inner side has an index. A hash join suits large, unsorted inputs joined on equality. A merge join is best when both inputs are already sorted on the join key.

column1: Why does a LEFT JOIN sometimes behave like an INNER JOIN?
column2: For unmatched rows, the right table's columns are NULL. A WHERE condition on those columns removes exactly those rows. To keep them, move the condition into the ON clause.
ROW_NUMBER gives a unique sequence (1,2,3,4). RANK lets ties share a rank and then leaves a gap (1,2,2,4). DENSE_RANK lets ties share a rank with no gap (1,2,2,3).

column1: How do you get the top N rows per group?
column2: In a subquery or CTE, rank rows with PARTITION BY group ORDER BY metric DESC. Then, in the outer query, keep only rows where the rank is N or less.

column1: How do you compute a running total?
column2: Use SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY t ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW). Write ROWS explicitly so tied values don't get the same total.

It is a CTE with two parts: an anchor query that gives the starting rows, and a recursive query that refers back to the CTE. The engine repeats the recursive part until no new rows come out. It is used for hierarchies.

Usually no. Modern PostgreSQL and SQL Server inline them, so they run like normal subqueries. Their real benefit is readability. In PostgreSQL, use MATERIALIZED when you deliberately want the CTE computed once.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation.

column1: Why can't I use a SELECT alias in WHERE?
column2: In the logical order, WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet. Either repeat the expression in WHERE, or wrap the query and filter outside.

column1: How does a B+ tree index speed up queries?
column2: It keeps keys sorted in a tree that is shallow and very wide. So a lookup reads only about 3–4 pages. Its leaves are linked together, so range scans read them one after another.
A clustered index stores the table rows themselves in key order, so there can be only one per table. A non-clustered index is a separate structure that points to the rows.

column1: Why might the database not use my index?
column2: Common reasons: a function or type conversion on the column, a leading wildcard, low selectivity, the wrong composite column order, stale statistics, or a bad cached plan.

column1: How do you choose composite index column order?
column2: Put equality filters first, then range or sort columns. Respect the leftmost-prefix rule. Add INCLUDE columns so the index covers the whole query.

column1: How would you find and fix a slow query?
column2: First find it, using the slow log, Query Store or APM. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare estimated rows with actual rows. Then fix indexes or rewrite the filters, return less data, and remove N+1 patterns. If needed, pre-aggregate or partition. Finally, confirm the improvement with metrics.
EXPLAIN shows the planned strategy with estimates only. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports the real rows and timings for each step.
Writers create new versions of a row instead of overwriting it. Readers see a consistent snapshot. So reads and writes don't block each other. Old versions are cleaned up later.

column1: How do database deadlocks happen and how do you handle them?
column2: Transactions wait on each other's row locks in a cycle, and the database aborts one of them. Prevent it with a consistent lock order, short transactions, good indexes and single-statement updates. Retry the victim.

column1: What is write skew and how do you prevent it?
column2: Two concurrent transactions read overlapping data. Based on it, each writes a different row, and together they break a rule (an invariant). Prevent it with SERIALIZABLE isolation, or by locking the rows you read with FOR UPDATE.

column1: What does FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED do?
column2: It locks the selected rows and skips any rows already locked by others. So parallel workers each grab different work items without blocking each other.
For read-heavy paths where joins cost too much, for analytics, for cached aggregates, and for historical snapshots such as the price at order time.

Partitioning splits a table inside one database, so queries can skip partitions and old data is easy to drop. Sharding spreads data across many database servers, to get more capacity and more write throughput.

A row store keeps each row together, which is ideal for transactional point reads and writes. A column store keeps each column together, which is ideal for scanning and aggregating a few columns over many rows, with high compression.

column1: Why is ClickHouse fast for aggregations?
column2: It uses columnar storage, so it reads only the needed columns. Data is heavily compressed. Data is sorted by the primary key, and a sparse index lets it skip granules. It uses vectorised execution. And materialised views pre-aggregate data at insert time.
Distributed SQL across many data sources, without storing any data itself. It is used for ad-hoc analytics across a data lake and operational databases.

column1: How do you generate short codes without collisions at scale?
column2: Give each instance its own pre-allocated range of IDs and encode them in base62. (Snowflake or UUIDv7 IDs, encoded, also work.) This way, no request needs to coordinate with other machines.
A 301 is cached by browsers. That means less load on you, but you lose analytics because repeat clicks never reach you. A 302 lets you see every click. Choose based on whether analytics matter.

column1: How do you keep redirects fast while counting clicks?
column2: Serve the redirect from the cache. Publish click events in the background to Kafka, and count them there.

column1: How do you make the limiter atomic across instances?
column2: Keep the state in Redis and update it with a Lua script. Then read, check and write all happen in one atomic operation.

column1: What happens if Redis is down?
column2: It is a deliberate policy decision. For normal APIs, fail open and use approximate local limits. For sensitive endpoints, fail closed. Either way, raise an alert.
Use token bucket when you want to allow controlled bursts while keeping a smooth average rate. Use a sliding window counter for simple, accurate limits per time window.

column1: How do you ensure OTPs aren't delayed by a marketing campaign?
column2: Give each priority its own topics, its own consumer pools and its own provider quotas. Also shape (throttle) the rate of bulk traffic.

column1: How do you avoid sending duplicate notifications?
column2: Use an idempotency key per (event, user, channel). Store it with a TTL and a unique constraint. Also make the webhook handling idempotent.
Keep a status machine for each message, updated by provider callbacks. Store it in a store built for heavy writes, with dashboards showing delivery rates per provider.
Push makes reads cheap but makes writes expensive for popular authors. Pull is the opposite. Use a hybrid: push for most users, pull for celebrities.

column1: How do you paginate a feed that changes constantly?
column2: Use a cursor based on (score or timestamp, postId), not page offsets. Offsets break when new posts are added at the top.

column1: How do you route a message to a user connected to a different server?
column2: Keep a session registry in Redis that maps each user to their connection server. Then send the message to that server through internal pub/sub or a direct RPC call.

column1: How do you guarantee ordering and no loss?
column2: Save the message before acking. Assign a sequence number per conversation. Make sends idempotent using client message IDs. On reconnect, resync from the last seen sequence.
The write volume is very high, and messages are read by conversation in time order. That fits Cassandra's partition key + clustering key model well, and Cassandra scales out by adding machines.

column1: How would you scale a cache horizontally?
column2: Split keys across nodes with consistent hashing or hash slots. Add replicas for failover, and let the client route each key to the right node.

column1: Why is Redis single-threaded yet fast?
column2: In-memory operations take microseconds. A single thread avoids lock contention and context switches. And I/O multiplexing (one thread watching many sockets) lets it serve many connections at once.

column1: How do you prevent duplicate accruals when Kafka redelivers?
column2: Keep a unique constraint on the processed event ID (or idempotency key), and write it in the same transaction as the ledger entry. A redelivered event then fails the constraint and is skipped.

column1: What if the voucher partner fails after points are debited?
column2: The saga retries with the same idempotency key, so the partner never issues two vouchers. If the failure is permanent, the saga compensates: it credits the points back and marks the redemption failed.

column1: How do you keep balance reads fast?
column2: Keep a cached balance column that is updated in the same transaction as the ledger. Add Redis on top, evicted whenever the balance changes. Serve statements from read replicas.

column1: How do you avoid double charging?
column2: Use idempotency keys at every hop — from client to API, and from API to PSP. Make state changes conditional, so a repeat does nothing. And when the outcome is unknown, ask the PSP for the status instead of retrying blindly.
Every movement balances debits and credits. So errors show up immediately, balances can be calculated from the entries, and the full history can be audited.

column1: What if the PSP webhook never arrives?
column2: A poller asks the PSP for the status of payments that have been pending too long. Daily reconciliation against the settlement files catches anything still missed.

column1: Which data structure would you use?
column2: A sorted set built on a skip list — Redis ZSETs. Score updates and rank lookups are O(log n), and fetching the top k is O(log n + k).

column1: How do you scale beyond one Redis node?
column2: Shard the users. For the global top k, merge each shard's top k. For a global rank, estimate it using histograms of scores.

column1: How do you make suggestions fast?
column2: Keep a trie in memory with the top-K precomputed at each node. Add edge and client caching, and debounce requests so you don't call on every keystroke.

column1: How do you keep suggestions fresh?
column2: Rebuild from the logs in regular batches, and merge in a small real-time trending layer at query time.

column1: Why a columnar store for metrics and logs?
column2: Queries read only a few columns, but across huge time ranges. A columnar store reads just those columns, compresses them well and scans them in vectorised batches (many values at once). So these aggregations are fast and cheap.

column1: How do you handle 10× traffic bursts?
column2: Kafka buffers the burst. Consumers scale up based on lag (how far behind they are). Ingestion applies per-tenant rate limits and sampling.

column1: How do you ensure a job runs once even with multiple scheduler nodes?
column2: Two layers. First, claiming is atomic: schedulers select due rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (or own partitions through leases), create the run and move next_run_at forward in the same transaction — so a slot can be claimed only once. Second, delivery is still at-least-once (queue redelivery, worker crashes), so each run has an execution_id = job + scheduled time with a UNIQUE constraint, and handlers are idempotent. Together: effectively once.

column1: How do you scale to millions of near-term jobs?
column2: Keep definitions in a DB with a partial index on next_run_at. Partition jobs into buckets by hash and give each scheduler a lease on some buckets. Pre-load jobs due in the next few minutes into a Redis sorted set or a timing wheel so the DB is not polled every second. Publish runs to a queue and scale workers separately based on queue lag. Spread fixed-time peaks with jitter.

column1: A worker picks up a job and dies halfway. What happens?
column2: The worker holds a lease on the run and renews it with heartbeats. When it dies, the lease expires; a reaper finds the run and re-queues it as the next attempt. Because the handler is idempotent and saves checkpoints, the retry continues safely without double effects.

column1: The whole system was down for 4 hours. What happens to jobs that should have run?
column2: Their next_run_at is in the past, so they are due immediately. The per-job misfire policy decides: run once to catch up (cleanup jobs), run every missed slot (per-period billing), or skip to the next slot (time-sensitive notifications). Also throttle the catch-up so the backlog doesn't overload downstream systems.

column1: How do you handle time zones and daylight saving time?
column2: Store the IANA zone name with the job and always store next_run_at in UTC. Compute the next time with the cron expression in the job's zone, then convert to UTC. Define policy for the DST gap (move forward) and overlap (run at the first occurrence) and test both dates.

column1: Why put a queue between schedulers and workers?
column2: It separates "when" from "how". Schedulers stay small and fast; workers can be slow, many and autoscaled. The queue absorbs peaks, gives retries and a DLQ, and lets you route jobs by priority or tenant. Without it, a slow job would block the scheduler loop and delay every other job.

column1: When would you not build this, and use something off the shelf?
column2: For a few fixed jobs in one service, @Scheduled + ShedLock or a Kubernetes CronJob is enough. For long multi-step workflows, Temporal; for data pipelines with dependencies, Airflow; for clustered Java scheduling at moderate scale, Quartz. Build your own when you need millions of user-defined, multi-tenant schedules with custom misfire, fairness and retry policies.

column1: How do you find nearby drivers efficiently?
column2: Keep a geo index (geohash, H3 or quadtree) of current locations in memory. Search the rider's cell first, then the rings of neighbouring cells.

column1: How do you prevent two riders getting the same driver?
column2: Change the driver's status atomically before sending the offer — with Redis SET NX, CAS (compare-and-set), or a conditional update. Release the driver if they decline or the offer times out.

column1: How would you handle 250k location updates per second?
column2: Keep only the latest location per driver, in memory, sharded by city. Write the stream to Kafka for history. Avoid a synchronous DB write for each update.
Streaming gives users timely progress. Batch over the source of truth guarantees payouts that are correct and can be reproduced, even when data arrives late or gets corrected.

column1: How do you handle a scheme changed mid-month?
column2: I version the scheme definitions. Each period is evaluated with the version that was effective for it. I also show users which version applies to them.

column1: How do you handle uploads at scale?
column2: Clients upload directly to object storage using pre-signed URLs. Storage events trigger background processing pipelines. Metadata goes into the database, and the media is delivered through a CDN.

column1: How do you count likes on a viral post?
column2: I use sharded counters in Redis and add them up into the database from time to time. A separate likes table answers "did I like it?".

column1: How does adaptive bitrate streaming work?
column2: The video is encoded into several renditions (qualities). Each is split into short segments, listed in a manifest. The player chooses a rendition for each segment based on bandwidth and how full its buffer is.
Split the video into segments. Encode them in parallel across a fleet of workers, organised as a DAG. Then package and publish.

column1: How would you detect trending topics?
column2: A stream processor keeps sliding-window counts per term and per region. Each term is scored by how fast it is rising compared with its normal baseline. Approximate structures like Count-Min Sketch keep this cheap.

column1: How do you decide when to assign a delivery partner?
column2: I use the predicted food-ready time and the partner's travel time, so the partner arrives just as the food is ready. I re-check this as the estimates change.
Almost every operation stays inside one city. Partitioning by city limits the *blast radius* — how far a failure spreads — and lets each city scale on its own.
With an atomic conditional decrement or reservation at the source of truth — a database conditional update, or a Redis Lua script. I add reservation TTLs and reconciliation on top.

column1: How do you survive the flash-sale spike?
column2: I shape the traffic before it reaches the backend, using a CDN, a waiting room and rate limits. Buyers are admitted through fast atomic counters in Redis. Orders are then created asynchronously, at a rate the system can sustain.

column1: What if payment succeeds but order creation fails?
column2: The payment-success event drives an idempotent retry of order creation — retrying is safe and never creates two orders. If it still can't complete, the system refunds automatically.
